info.name: SE3090 Lecture 04 - LankaMart (PostgreSQL, JWT, RBAC)
info.description:
Teaching collection for SE3090 Lecture 04: Database Design, Authentication, Authorization and Integration.

HOW TO USE
1. Start the API:  dotnet run --project src/LankaMart.Api
2. Run '2.1 Login as Amal (Customer)' - the test script stores the token in a collection variable, so every later request is already authenticated.
3. Work down the folders in order. Folder 3 is the heart of the lecture: same endpoint, different caller, different answer.

Or use the Collection Runner: it will run every request and report pass/fail on each assertion.

item.name: 1. Public endpoints (no token)
item.description: Everything here works with no Authorization header at all. Browsing a catalogue should not require an account.

request.description: Watch the terminal: EF Core prints the SELECT, the COUNT and the LIMIT/OFFSET it sent to PostgreSQL.
The search becomes an ILIKE in SQL - the value is parameterized, never concatenated (slide 40).
Slide 18: categories are a table now, so products reference them by id.
Slide 23: check current_user. If it says 'postgres', the API is connected as the superuser and one injection flaw becomes catastrophic.

item.name: 2. Authentication (slides 30-33)
item.description: Obtaining, reading, rotating and revoking tokens.

request.description: Run this FIRST. The test script stores accessToken and refreshToken as collection variables for every request below.
Stores staffToken.
Stores adminToken.
Needed for the 403 demo in folder 3 - two customers with identical roles and different data.
Note the message, then compare with 2.6. They are identical on purpose: different messages let an attacker enumerate registered emails.
The assertion below is the lesson: the two failure messages must match.

request.description: Slide 31 step 6. Nothing here reads the database - this identity came entirely from the signed token.

exec: pm.test("the token carried a role", function () {

request.description: 401 means UNAUTHENTICATED: we do not know who you are (slide 28).
The payload claims Admin, but the signature does not match. This is what the signing key protects (slide 30).

item.name: 2.10 Decode a token with no key

request.description: Signed, not encrypted. Anyone can read a JWT; only the key holder can forge one. Therefore no secrets in the payload (slide 30).
Issues a new pair and REVOKES the presented token. Single use, always.

exec: pm.test("a different refresh token came back", function () {

item.name: 2.12 Replay the OLD refresh token -> 401 + family revoked

request.description: Run 2.11 first, then this. It presents the SAME token again - exactly what a thief would do. The API cannot tell theft from replay, so it revokes the entire family and forces a fresh login. Check the terminal for 'Refresh token REUSE detected' (slide 32).
This body asks for the Admin role. RegisterRequest has no such field, so there is nowhere for it to bind and it is silently ignored (slide 40).

exec: pm.test("only the Customer role was granted", function () {

item.name: 3. Authorization - the heart of the lecture (slides 36-38)
item.description: Same endpoint, same valid token, different caller, different answer. Run 2.1 to 2.4 first so all four tokens exist.

request.description: No customerId in the body. It comes from the 'sub' claim of the token, server-side (slide 33, last row).
The same request, now claiming customerId 1 and DELIVERED status. Check the response: the order belongs to the TOKEN, not to the body.

exec: pm.test("customerId came from the token, not the body", function () {

request.description: No id in the route, so there is nothing to tamper with. The safest possible design for a per-user resource.

THE demo. Order 1 belongs to Amal. Ask for it as Nadia: valid token, identical Customer role, same endpoint - and 403. Broken object-level authorization is number one in the OWASP API Security Top 10 (slide 36). See OrderService.EnsureCanAccess.

item.name: 3.5 The same order, as its owner -> 200

request.description: Ownership, not role, is what changed.
Staff handle every order. Role beats ownership here, by design.
Authenticated and refused: 403, not 401 (slide 28).
[Authorize(Roles = "Staff,Admin")] on the action (slide 38).
Slide 38, line by line. The request never reaches the action body.
Same URL, same body, different token.
A narrower role list on a more destructive verb.
Allowed - as long as the product has never been ordered.
ON DELETE RESTRICT on order_items -> products. PostgreSQL refuses to let the application shred an invoice, and SQLSTATE 23503 becomes a clean 409 (slides 14 and 26).
Guarded by a POLICY requiring the 'orders.refund' permission claim, not by a role list (slide 38, bottom note).
No permission claim in this token.
Slide 37 - the junction table, rendered as JSON.
ONE row inserted into user_roles. Nothing on the users row changes.

item.name: 3.18 *** Revocation lag *** re-run 3.9 with the OLD token

request.description: Amal is Staff now, but his current access token was signed before the grant and still says Customer - so this is STILL 403. Log in again (2.1) and it works. That is the cost of stateless auth (slide 37).
This also revokes Amal's refresh tokens, so the removal cannot be outlived by a quiet renewal.

item.name: 4. Validation, errors and the deliberately wrong code
item.description: Slides 26, 40 and 41. The demo endpoints return 404 unless the API is in Development with EnableTeachingEndpoints = true.

request.description: Empty name, negative price. Rejected by [ApiController] before any of our code runs, with a field-by-field list.
Well-formed request, impossible outcome: more units than we hold. 409, not 400.
A real unique-violation from the database, translated into a clean Problem Details document (slide 26).
No stack trace, no table names, no file paths - just a traceId you can find in the log (slide 41).
